title: The Army That Lost a War to Birds #shorts

lines.text: An army rolled out machine guns to fight a bunch of birds.
Farmers out west were furious. Twenty thousand emus were stomping through their wheat and eating everything.
So the army sent a major, two soldiers, two machine guns, and crates and crates of bullets.
Everyone figured this would be easy. They're birds. How hard can it be?
Then the first flock showed up, and the soldiers opened fire.
The emus scattered in every direction, like somebody kicked a bag of marbles.
So they set up an ambush by a water hole. A thousand emus came strolling right toward them.
Fine. They tied a machine gun to a truck and chased them.
But the emus ran faster than the truck, and the ride was so bumpy the gunner couldn't even aim.
Newspapers made fun of them. Lawmakers asked if the soldiers would get medals for surviving.
You see, emus don't march in a line like an army. Every flock had a tall lookout, and the moment anything went bang, they split up.
It's like trying to swat a hundred flies with one rolled up newspaper.
The major even admitted these birds could take bullets like tanks.
After about five weeks, the army packed up and went home.
Thousands of bullets later, the emus were still eating the wheat.
And the major's official report proudly said his men suffered no casualties.

sources: Wikipedia, 'Emu War': late 1932, Campion district, Western Australia; Major G.P.W. Meredith with Sergeant McMurray and Gunner O'Halloran, two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds; about 20,000 emus damaging wheat; the first flock scattered; an ambush at a dam with about 1,000 emus ended when the gun jammed; a gun mounted on a truck could not keep up and the ride was too rough to fire; each flock had a tall lookout; troops withdrawn 8 November, second attempt 13 November to 10 December (986 confirmed kills with 9,860 rounds); the official report noted no casualties among the men; Meredith said the birds could face machine guns 'with the invulnerability of tanks'
Mental Floss, 'When Australia Went to War With Its Emus': 2,500 rounds by 8 November for as few as 50 birds; press ridicule; Pearce ended the first operation
Canada Bay Heritage Society, 'Australia's Emu War': the House of Representatives asked whether medals would be awarded to survivors of the campaign
Australian Geographic, 'Looking back: Australia's Emu Wars': recalled within a week of first contact; no casualties among the men
